Homeschooling under threat

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Homeschooling was legalised in 1996. But a new bill is about to change the face of home education giving the state the power to dictate how homeschooling should be done. We have the story.

Unique Selling Point:
Since 1996, more than 54 000 families have provided home education for their children. The movement to homeschooling has been the result of parents being dissatisfied with the quality of teaching and feeling that public education does not prepare their children for professional careers.

Prior to 2017, homeschooling was not regulated by the state. Then in 2017, the Department of Basic Education or DBE made a sudden announcement proposing drastic changes to the homeschooling policy. His motivation for the changes, he said, was to regulate the environment, provide guidelines and make sure that homeschooling is legislated. The nuts and bolts of this new legislation, however, will remove parents’ freedom of choice and make the state co-parents of home education.

The key changes as outlined in the Basic Education Laws Amendment (BELA) Bill are: parents have to apply to homeschool and go through a stringent process, an official will visit the home to check that the environment is similar to a classroom situation, only government-approved curriculums will be accepted; a child’s progress will be assessed annually by a government assessor at huge additional cost to the parent, and parents must keep a register of their child’s attendance.

There was an immediate backlash from parents. Why is the state interfering with a process that has been successful over the last 22 years, they wanted to know. Why is the state taking away parents’ constitutional right to decide what type of education their child should receive by becoming the co-parents of their children’s education at home? They contend that the amendment outlined in the Bill defeats the purpose of homeschooling in the first place. It will also place an extra financial burden on the state, which means the taxpayers, as well as the parents, who are already footing the bill of homeschooling in that one parent may be forfeiting a salary to stay at home and teach and homeschoolers need to buy the study material.

From the 13th of October 2017, when the announcement was made by the department, less than a month’s grace period was given for public comment. Despite many emails and public lobbying by the Pestalozzi Trust, acting on behalf of homeschooling families, comment closed on November, the 10th. The Bill is in the process of becoming an Act.


Summary:
Education in South Africa is the responsibility of the Department of Basic Education. Its vision statement is “to ensure learners from Grade R to Grade 12 have access to lifelong learning, education and training which will contribute towards improving the quality of life and building a peaceful, prosperous and democratic South Africa”. But the stats tells another story: Only a third of learners starting Grade 1 each year make it to their final matric exams. The department is simply not equipped to handle the growing number of learners annually resulting in overcrowded classrooms, poor quality of teaching and discipline problems.

These are some of the reasons many parents in South Africa have chosen to go the homeschooling route. With home education, parents take ownership over their children’s learning process and create an environment where each child is given the best opportunity to grow according to his or her needs and personality.


Further information:
Nandi Msezane is a single mother from Randburg who has opted for homeschooling her son, Voyo. She felt public schooling was not giving him the best chances in life. Eleven-year-old Voyo is crazy about soccer and an over-achiever by nature. His personality requires stimulation and goal setting, something Msezane says public school were lack. Msezane, who is a project manager, has managed to spend quality time with her son and still pursue her career. Schooling Voyo came naturally to her. She has made the classroom a fun learning environment with a few quality hours per day rather than endless lessons that leave a child learning by rote. Since Msezane started homeschooling two years ago, she has set up a community Facebook page called Browny Homeschoolers of South Africa for black parents, promoting a pan-African ideology. In just two year, her group has grown from 10 families to over 100, all sharing a common goal of personalised tutoring.

The Shelver family from Cape Town’s northern suburbs has two children who are both homeschooled. Duncan, 17, wants to become a magician and has prepared himself for his future by taking extra classes from the College of Magic. He thrives on setting his own goals and achieving them. He is already a decision maker preparing for a successful career. His younger sister, Jody, on the other hand prefers structured learning and will diligently work her day into lessons she enjoys, says mom, Louise. “My children are both so different and I enjoy the challenge of tailor-making their studies. Her husband works so Louise has taken on the role of homeschool mom.

Shameela Safodien, a psychologist from Durbanville, also in Cape Town, has chosen to homeschool her two daughters. The youngest, 7-year-old Nurah, was a particular concern to Safodien as she was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder called selective mutism: it means a child is unable to read or speak aloud in class as she cannot verbalise her thoughts. Nurah has taken to homeschooling like a duck to water and enjoys the informal atmosphere, interacting with her mother in the kitchen, while learning.

All three families we spoke to are concerned about the BELA Bill and the changes it will bring once enforced. “It is not in the interests of us as the parents to give the state control over the content we teach our children, the hours, the assessment which comes at a huge additional cost. It does not make sense,” says Louise Shelver. Msezane says: “The state cannot decide what education my child will have by forcing him into their curriculum.” Safodien feels forcing children back into an environment prescribed by the state is exactly what she chose not to do and cannot see why the department wants to saddle parents with the additional financial burden and restrictions of more aimless rules which do not add value to the child’s learning process.

Up to now, the cost of homeschooling was another benefit as the tutoring material could be selected according to affordability. By dictating that material, the government is forcing parents to enroll their children in the SA National Education Department curriculum or a similar curriculum that it approves. With so many international and local courses available online to select from, parents have been able to match their children’s interest with suitable subjects in which they can excel. Sadly, many of these courses are not in the government curriculum and children will therefore miss out.

We will put the department on the spot asking what motivated the proposed changes to the BELA Bill; what research studies were performed to assess homeschooling and on what they base their need for regulating homeschooling on, regulation that smacks of policing.

Bouwe van der Eems, chairman of the Pestalozzi Trust will discuss the dialogue at government level on behalf of parents to lobby against the proposed changes to the Bill. According to Van der Eem, not enough time for public comment was allowed and the department was not prepared to engage in meaningful discussions with the organisation or listen to the objections, but simply went ahead with the amendments, which are on the verge of being passed.
Background
Home education was illegal in South Africa during Apartheid. The punishment was severe: In 1994, an example was made out of parents Andre and Bokkie Meintjies who were jailed and their two children placed in an orphanage. It was only in 1996 that a new law was passed - Section 51 Act No 84 of the South African Schools Act - legalising home education. Since then, it has grown exponentially and is recognised as a successful proven alternative to public schooling. According to the Pestalozzi Trust, a national organisation providing legal advice and a support system to homeschooling parents, approximately 120 000 children are currently being home educated.

Homeschooling is legal in many countries. Countries with the most prevalent home education movements include Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Press Release:


Homeschooling at Risk
For years, thousands of parents have chosen to take their children out of mainstream public and private schools, for the benefit of learning and teaching at home. Now a new bill could change the face of home education, giving the state more power to dictate how homeschooling should be done. Carte Blanche explores this changing landscape.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe
Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


Script: Homeschooling at risk
Duration: 9 minutes

V/O Shamiela Safodien from Cape Town has been homeschooling her daughters Nurah and Aaliyah for the last 2 years. She has been able to pay special attention to Nurah, who has a learning disability.

Shaamiela Safodien: She was diagnosed with selective mutism which really just means she struggles to communicate effectively in certain settings; one of that settings is school.

V/O But now, homeschooling rules could change. The Department of Basic Education has introduced a bill to reform a number of aspects around education including what homeschooling parents may teach and how their children should be assessed.

LINK: The Department of Basic Education has proposed drastic changes to the homeschooling policy which many parents fear will take away their freedom of choice.

Shaamiela Safodien: Homeschooling parent - The immediate reaction is fear. I have made this decision and I am committed to it and really my heart is in this.

V/O Elijah Mhlanga, spokesperson for the Department of Basic Education says the department has been inundated with input and complaints from parents and organisations.

Elijah Mhlanga: We received about 5000 inputs. People have brought boxes here. We are going through each and everyone of those. We now have about 1900 in fact as I am speaking to you there is a team on another floor right now who are busy going through those inputs.

V/O Prior to 1996 homeschooling was illegal in South Africa. Parents could be jailed. 22 years later, parents are fighting for their rights again. This time it’s for the freedom to choose every aspect of homeschooling without the government’s interference. Bouwe van der Eems of the Pestalozzi Trust, a legal defense fund that lobbies for the rights of home education fears the new bill will give the state too much control over the process as well as the content.

Bouwe van der Eems: Chairman Pestalozzi Trust: Our concerns about the content is the current act says the education must meet certain minimum standards. If you prescribe content and skills it takes away the freedom of the parents to give their children the education that is needed for each individual child. Secondly it introduces regular assessments at the cost of the parents so that could make home education unaffordable and the assessments then also enforces the content and skills of the curriculum and thirdly the penalty for not registering has been increased from 6 months to 6 years.

Louise Shelver: Homeschooling parent - For us the biggest issue is having to ask permission to homeschool your child as parents we know our children and know what is best for our child.

Up audio

V/O Louise Shelver also from Cape Town has homeschooled her 15 year old daughter Toni and 17 year old son Duncan since primary school. The bill challenges everything they’ve become used to.

Claire Mawisa: How serious are you homeschoolers taking it?

Louise Shelver: Very serious. First of all for someone to say we must have permission to homeschool; to have to regulate what kind of curriculum we choose when there are so many different learning styles that we try and fit to our child’s choices; the assessing: we are not always with all subjects on a certain grade and also very important the people who make the rules and regulate and do the site visits, if they don't understand homeschooling they are not welcome in my house.

Claire Mawisa: One of the concerns is about the assessments parents have to pay for could you elaborate on that.

Elijah Mhlanga: Well it is very simple it is part of monitoring we need to make sure that learning is happening and there has to be an independent person assessing whether the child is progressing at the right level and he knows what he should know.

Claire Mawisa: How much am I be paying for?

Elijah Mhlanga: The province will determine that.

V/O Homeschoolers feel that the unique capabilities of their children might be disregarded by government assessors who would measure them against the national curriculum.

Nandi Msezane: Let us all be honest. The education system in SA has failed our children. The children who lose out the most are black children because the resources are not there in schools; there are not enough teachers; those classes are overcrowded.

V/O In Benoni, Nandi Msezane homeschools her 11 year old son Macky. For her, formal education did not speak to his African roots. She promotes a Pan-African approach to homeschooling which aims to build identity and self-esteem and sees education as a tool for development and community service.

Nandi Msezane: He is very interested in South Africa’s political past because of our own family history. As much as people like to talk about being colour blind we don’t live in a colour blind world. He sees racism he sees how people treat each other and so he wants to learn.

V/O Msezane has seen homeschooling grow in her community and has started a Facebook group to promote the pan-African educational perspective.

Nandi Msezane: We are now in the region of 100 black families. The department usually makes homeschooling seem like it is a white thing but there are more black families who have beginning to home educate.

V/O Msezane took the leap into home education four years ago when her son’s previous school demanded he shave off his dreadlocks.

Nandi Msezane: They told me his hair was contrary to the discipline of the school. When he was in grade three going onto grade four the school then said if he did not attend school sports they would get demerit affecting their actual education in class and I said ok it is time for us to part ways.

V/O Homeschooling allows parents the freedom to choose where and how learning takes place. Now Macky practices mathematics on the soccer field. He’s won multiple soccer trophies and often travels to compete.

Nandi Msezane. It works for us because my son travels for football so I don’t need to negotiate time off school. He is wanting to become a goalkeeper so our curriculum is centered around football so how he learns his science how he learns his math.

V/O If the new bill becomes law parents will have to take a daily attendance register. But possibly the crux of the homeschooler’s resistance to BELA is the government-approved curriculum.

Claire Mawisa: What is the prescribed curriculum for home education?

Elijah Mhlanga: It has to be consistent with the national curriculum statement which the department is using at the moment. The policy also makes provision for parents to choose the curriculum but we need to know about it so we know what to assess because if you don’t know what they are learning you will not be in a position to check where they are in terms of their development.

V/O Parents are also objecting to home inspectors, to check whether the learning environment is suitable for the child.

Elijah Mhlanga: We wanted to legalise that environment to make space for it but we also wanted to make sure that we protect the interest of the child. It involved going to the places because if you are registering someone you need to take responsibility for that so you have to make sure that what you have been told is indeed taking place.

V/O Safodien’s youngest, Nurah struggles to communicate effectively because of her anxiety in crowded places. For her, learning takes place casually in the kitchen. Safodien feels assessors will not be able to accurately assess her child and how she is learning and how she develops.

Shaamiela Safodien: She loves anything that involves intricacies, so building puzzles and she loves the kitchen. For me the big concerns is that there will be assessments that need to occur. They have not seen me engage with my children; they don't know their learning ability. And then the other big concern I have is of course the curriculum.

Claire: Why?

Shaamiela Safodien: I don't feel that the education department curriculum is necessary attending to that need. I am learning that Aaliyah learns in one way and Nurah in a different way.

Nandi Msezane: When I took on home educating my child I understood what kind of commitment I was making.

V/O For many homeschooling parents, forfeiting their right to choose their children’s education, is non-negotiable.

Shaamiela Safodien: The biggest support we could get is our constitutional right is being upheld that would be important to me.

Nandi: If the BELA bill gets passed if homeschooling becomes more restrictive in SA we have multiple choices one of which is pursuing a legal action.

Louise; It will take years and years to understand and respect what we do.

END

V/O There is an outcry amongst homeschooling parents as the government moves into final gear with a new bill that will restrict home educators.
Nandi Msezane: If the BELA bill gets passed we have multiple choices one of which is pursuing legal action.

15 seconds:
V/O Since 1996 thousands of families have turned to homeschooling. Now a new bill proposed by the government aims to regulate laws on parents who home educate.
Shaamiela Safodien: Of course, the immediate reaction is fear. I have made this decision and I am committed to it.

30 seconds
V/O Homeschooling is a growing movement among parents dissatisfied with the level of teaching in public schools. But legislation by the state could force parents back into government-approved curriculum which they feel is an infringement of their constitutional right to choose what is best for their children.
Shaamiela Safodien: The big concerns is that there will be assessments that need to occur. I don't feel that the education department curriculum is necessary attending to that need. And I want the freedom as a parent.

Producer: Annalise Lubbe Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: Script: Homeschooling at risk Duration: 9 minutes V/O Shamiela Safodien from Cape Town has been homeschooling her daughters Nurah and Aaliyah for the last 2 years. She has been able to pay special attention to Nurah, who has a learning disability. Shaamiela Safodien: She was diagnosed with selective mutism which really just means she struggles to communicate effectively in certain settings; one of that settings is school. V/O But now, homeschooling rules could change. The Department of Basic Education has introduced a bill to reform a number of aspects around education including what homeschooling parents may teach and how their children should be assessed. LINK: The Department of Basic Education has proposed drastic changes to the homeschooling policy which many parents fear will take away their freedom of choice. Shaamiela Safodien: Homeschooling parent - The immediate reaction is fear. I have made this decision and I am committed to it and really my heart is in this. V/O Elijah Mhlanga, spokesperson for the Department of Basic Education says the department has been inundated with input and complaints from parents and organisations. Elijah Mhlanga: We received about 5000 inputs. People have brought boxes here. We are going through each and everyone of those. We now have about 1900 in fact as I am speaking to you there is a team on another floor right now who are busy going through those inputs. V/O Prior to 1996 homeschooling was illegal in South Africa. Parents could be jailed. 22 years later, parents are fighting for their rights again. This time it’s for the freedom to choose every aspect of homeschooling without the government’s interference. Bouwe van der Eems of the Pestalozzi Trust, a legal defense fund that lobbies for the rights of home education fears the new bill will give the state too much control over the process as well as the content. Bouwe van der Eems: Chairman Pestalozzi Trust: Our concerns about the content is the current act says the education must meet certain minimum standards. If you prescribe content and skills it takes away the freedom of the parents to give their children the education that is needed for each individual child. Secondly it introduces regular assessments at the cost of the parents so that could make home education unaffordable and the assessments then also enforces the content and skills of the curriculum and thirdly the penalty for not registering has been increased from 6 months to 6 years. Louise Shelver: Homeschooling parent - For us the biggest issue is having to ask permission to homeschool your child as parents we know our children and know what is best for our child. Up audio V/O Louise Shelver also from Cape Town has homeschooled her 15 year old daughter Toni and 17 year old son Duncan since primary school. The bill challenges everything they’ve become used to. Claire Mawisa: How serious are you homeschoolers taking it? Louise Shelver: Very serious. First of all for someone to say we must have permission to homeschool; to have to regulate what kind of curriculum we choose when there are so many different learning styles that we try and fit to our child’s choices; the assessing: we are not always with all subjects on a certain grade and also very important the people who make the rules and regulate and do the site visits, if they don't understand homeschooling they are not welcome in my house. Claire Mawisa: One of the concerns is about the assessments parents have to pay for could you elaborate on that. Elijah Mhlanga: Well it is very simple it is part of monitoring we need to make sure that learning is happening and there has to be an independent person assessing whether the child is progressing at the right level and he knows what he should know. Claire Mawisa: How much am I be paying for? Elijah Mhlanga: The province will determine that. V/O Homeschoolers feel that the unique capabilities of their children might be disregarded by government assessors who would measure them against the national curriculum. Nandi Msezane: Let us all be honest. The education system in SA has failed our children. The children who lose out the most are black children because the resources are not there in schools; there are not enough teachers; those classes are overcrowded. V/O In Benoni, Nandi Msezane homeschools her 11 year old son Macky. For her, formal education did not speak to his African roots. She promotes a Pan-African approach to homeschooling which aims to build identity and self-esteem and sees education as a tool for development and community service. Nandi Msezane: He is very interested in South Africa’s political past because of our own family history. As much as people like to talk about being colour blind we don’t live in a colour blind world. He sees racism he sees how people treat each other and so he wants to learn. V/O Msezane has seen homeschooling grow in her community and has started a Facebook group to promote the pan-African educational perspective. Nandi Msezane: We are now in the region of 100 black families. The department usually makes homeschooling seem like it is a white thing but there are more black families who have beginning to home educate. V/O Msezane took the leap into home education four years ago when her son’s previous school demanded he shave off his dreadlocks. Nandi Msezane: They told me his hair was contrary to the discipline of the school. When he was in grade three going onto grade four the school then said if he did not attend school sports they would get demerit affecting their actual education in class and I said ok it is time for us to part ways. V/O Homeschooling allows parents the freedom to choose where and how learning takes place. Now Macky practices mathematics on the soccer field. He’s won multiple soccer trophies and often travels to compete. Nandi Msezane. It works for us because my son travels for football so I don’t need to negotiate time off school. He is wanting to become a goalkeeper so our curriculum is centered around football so how he learns his science how he learns his math. V/O If the new bill becomes law parents will have to take a daily attendance register. But possibly the crux of the homeschooler’s resistance to BELA is the government-approved curriculum. Claire Mawisa: What is the prescribed curriculum for home education? Elijah Mhlanga: It has to be consistent with the national curriculum statement which the department is using at the moment. The policy also makes provision for parents to choose the curriculum but we need to know about it so we know what to assess because if you don’t know what they are learning you will not be in a position to check where they are in terms of their development. V/O Parents are also objecting to home inspectors, to check whether the learning environment is suitable for the child. Elijah Mhlanga: We wanted to legalise that environment to make space for it but we also wanted to make sure that we protect the interest of the child. It involved going to the places because if you are registering someone you need to take responsibility for that so you have to make sure that what you have been told is indeed taking place. V/O Safodien’s youngest, Nurah struggles to communicate effectively because of her anxiety in crowded places. For her, learning takes place casually in the kitchen. Safodien feels assessors will not be able to accurately assess her child and how she is learning and how she develops. Shaamiela Safodien: She loves anything that involves intricacies, so building puzzles and she loves the kitchen. For me the big concerns is that there will be assessments that need to occur. They have not seen me engage with my children; they don't know their learning ability. And then the other big concern I have is of course the curriculum. Claire: Why? Shaamiela Safodien: I don't feel that the education department curriculum is necessary attending to that need. I am learning that Aaliyah learns in one way and Nurah in a different way. Nandi Msezane: When I took on home educating my child I understood what kind of commitment I was making. V/O For many homeschooling parents, forfeiting their right to choose their children’s education, is non-negotiable. Shaamiela Safodien: The biggest support we could get is our constitutional right is being upheld that would be important to me. Nandi: If the BELA bill gets passed if homeschooling becomes more restrictive in SA we have multiple choices one of which is pursuing a legal action. Louise; It will take years and years to understand and respect what we do. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Homeschooling was legalised in 1996. But a new bill is about to change the face of home education giving the state the power to dictate how homeschooling should be done. We have the story.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Since 1996, more than 54 000 families have provided home education for their children. The movement to homeschooling has been the result of parents being dissatisfied with the quality of teaching and feeling that public education does not prepare their children for professional careers. Prior to 2017, homeschooling was not regulated by the state. Then in 2017, the Department of Basic Education or DBE made a sudden announcement proposing drastic changes to the homeschooling policy. His motivation for the changes, he said, was to regulate the environment, provide guidelines and make sure that homeschooling is legislated. The nuts and bolts of this new legislation, however, will remove parents’ freedom of choice and make the state co-parents of home education. The key changes as outlined in the Basic Education Laws Amendment (BELA) Bill are: parents have to apply to homeschool and go through a stringent process, an official will visit the home to check that the environment is similar to a classroom situation, only government-approved curriculums will be accepted; a child’s progress will be assessed annually by a government assessor at huge additional cost to the parent, and parents must keep a register of their child’s attendance. There was an immediate backlash from parents. Why is the state interfering with a process that has been successful over the last 22 years, they wanted to know. Why is the state taking away parents’ constitutional right to decide what type of education their child should receive by becoming the co-parents of their children’s education at home? They contend that the amendment outlined in the Bill defeats the purpose of homeschooling in the first place. It will also place an extra financial burden on the state, which means the taxpayers, as well as the parents, who are already footing the bill of homeschooling in that one parent may be forfeiting a salary to stay at home and teach and homeschoolers need to buy the study material. From the 13th of October 2017, when the announcement was made by the department, less than a month’s grace period was given for public comment. Despite many emails and public lobbying by the Pestalozzi Trust, acting on behalf of homeschooling families, comment closed on November, the 10th. The Bill is in the process of becoming an Act.
metadata.Summary: Education in South Africa is the responsibility of the Department of Basic Education. Its vision statement is “to ensure learners from Grade R to Grade 12 have access to lifelong learning, education and training which will contribute towards improving the quality of life and building a peaceful, prosperous and democratic South Africa”. But the stats tells another story: Only a third of learners starting Grade 1 each year make it to their final matric exams. The department is simply not equipped to handle the growing number of learners annually resulting in overcrowded classrooms, poor quality of teaching and discipline problems. These are some of the reasons many parents in South Africa have chosen to go the homeschooling route. With home education, parents take ownership over their children’s learning process and create an environment where each child is given the best opportunity to grow according to his or her needs and personality.
metadata.Further information: Nandi Msezane is a single mother from Randburg who has opted for homeschooling her son, Voyo. She felt public schooling was not giving him the best chances in life. Eleven-year-old Voyo is crazy about soccer and an over-achiever by nature. His personality requires stimulation and goal setting, something Msezane says public school were lack. Msezane, who is a project manager, has managed to spend quality time with her son and still pursue her career. Schooling Voyo came naturally to her. She has made the classroom a fun learning environment with a few quality hours per day rather than endless lessons that leave a child learning by rote. Since Msezane started homeschooling two years ago, she has set up a community Facebook page called Browny Homeschoolers of South Africa for black parents, promoting a pan-African ideology. In just two year, her group has grown from 10 families to over 100, all sharing a common goal of personalised tutoring. The Shelver family from Cape Town’s northern suburbs has two children who are both homeschooled. Duncan, 17, wants to become a magician and has prepared himself for his future by taking extra classes from the College of Magic. He thrives on setting his own goals and achieving them. He is already a decision maker preparing for a successful career. His younger sister, Jody, on the other hand prefers structured learning and will diligently work her day into lessons she enjoys, says mom, Louise. “My children are both so different and I enjoy the challenge of tailor-making their studies. Her husband works so Louise has taken on the role of homeschool mom. Shameela Safodien, a psychologist from Durbanville, also in Cape Town, has chosen to homeschool her two daughters. The youngest, 7-year-old Nurah, was a particular concern to Safodien as she was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder called selective mutism: it means a child is unable to read or speak aloud in class as she cannot verbalise her thoughts. Nurah has taken to homeschooling like a duck to water and enjoys the informal atmosphere, interacting with her mother in the kitchen, while learning. All three families we spoke to are concerned about the BELA Bill and the changes it will bring once enforced. “It is not in the interests of us as the parents to give the state control over the content we teach our children, the hours, the assessment which comes at a huge additional cost. It does not make sense,” says Louise Shelver. Msezane says: “The state cannot decide what education my child will have by forcing him into their curriculum.” Safodien feels forcing children back into an environment prescribed by the state is exactly what she chose not to do and cannot see why the department wants to saddle parents with the additional financial burden and restrictions of more aimless rules which do not add value to the child’s learning process. Up to now, the cost of homeschooling was another benefit as the tutoring material could be selected according to affordability. By dictating that material, the government is forcing parents to enroll their children in the SA National Education Department curriculum or a similar curriculum that it approves. With so many international and local courses available online to select from, parents have been able to match their children’s interest with suitable subjects in which they can excel. Sadly, many of these courses are not in the government curriculum and children will therefore miss out. We will put the department on the spot asking what motivated the proposed changes to the BELA Bill; what research studies were performed to assess homeschooling and on what they base their need for regulating homeschooling on, regulation that smacks of policing. Bouwe van der Eems, chairman of the Pestalozzi Trust will discuss the dialogue at government level on behalf of parents to lobby against the proposed changes to the Bill. According to Van der Eem, not enough time for public comment was allowed and the department was not prepared to engage in meaningful discussions with the organisation or listen to the objections, but simply went ahead with the amendments, which are on the verge of being passed. Background Home education was illegal in South Africa during Apartheid. The punishment was severe: In 1994, an example was made out of parents Andre and Bokkie Meintjies who were jailed and their two children placed in an orphanage. It was only in 1996 that a new law was passed - Section 51 Act No 84 of the South African Schools Act - legalising home education. Since then, it has grown exponentially and is recognised as a successful proven alternative to public schooling. According to the Pestalozzi Trust, a national organisation providing legal advice and a support system to homeschooling parents, approximately 120 000 children are currently being home educated. Homeschooling is legal in many countries. Countries with the most prevalent home education movements include Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.
